opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so with WebGPT, the setup was pretty narrow. You'd ask a question, the model would go off and browse, collect some sources, and then write up an answer with citations. And it worked reasonably well, but when we looked at how people actually wanted to use it, a lot of the value was in the follow-ups. You'd get an answer and then you'd want to say, "Wait, what about this?" or "Can you clarify that part?" or "That source looks wrong." The single-shot question-answering format was kind of artificial. Real information-seeking is iterative.

There was also a more technical motivation. One of the big problems we were wrestling with was truthfulness and grounding: getting the model to not just make stuff up. And it seemed like a lot of the failure cases were things where, if you could just have a back-and-forth, the human could catch the mistake, or the model could ask for clarification instead of guessing. So dialogue felt like a more natural interface for getting the model to be honest about uncertainty and to correct itself.

And then I think there was a sense that chat is just a really general interface. If you can make a model that's good at conversation, following instructions, answering questions, admitting when it doesn't know something, pushing back on a false premise, then you've kind of covered a huge range of use cases with one product. Browsing could be one tool it uses, but the core thing is the assistant. So we started working on a chat model, initially with the idea that retrieval would be a big part of it. As it turned out, the base model plus the RLHF fine-tuning was already pretty capable on its own without browsing, so the browsing part got de-emphasized for a while.

Honestly, I don't think any of us anticipated how much people would just enjoy talking to it. We thought of it as a research preview, a way to get feedback and learn about failure modes. The reaction was a lot bigger than we expected.

r001.rationale: It says users wanted to ask follow-ups and that single-shot question answering felt artificial.

r002.rationale: It says dialogue would let the model ask for clarification instead of guessing.

r003.rationale: It says the base model with RLHF was capable on its own without browsing, so browsing was de-emphasized.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so WebGPT was this project where we fine-tuned GPT-3 to answer questions by browsing the web, and we trained it with human feedback to produce answers with citations. And it worked reasonably well for that narrow task. But the thing that really stuck with me was that the question-answering setup felt artificial. People don't actually want to ask a single question and get a single polished answer. They want to follow up, they want to clarify, they want to say "no, that's not what I meant." So the single-turn format was kind of a toy version of the real problem.

The other thing we noticed was that a lot of the value wasn't really coming from the browsing. The model already knew a huge amount, and the browsing was useful for recent events or very specific facts, but for most of what people wanted to ask, the knowledge was already in the weights. So it seemed like the browsing was sort of a distraction from the more fundamental capability, which was: can you have a model that just talks to you, understands what you want, and is helpful and honest across a wide range of tasks?

And chat as a format has some nice properties for that. It's very general. Almost any task can be phrased as a conversation. It also makes the human feedback problem more tractable in some ways, because the raters are judging a response in context, and the model can ask for clarification instead of guessing. Also, around that time we were doing RLHF on instruction following with the InstructGPT line of work, and it felt like the natural synthesis was: take the RLHF methodology we'd been developing, apply it to multi-turn dialogue, and drop the requirement that the model ground everything in search results. So it was less a huge leap and more that WebGPT made it pretty obvious that dialogue was where the actual product and the actual research questions were.

r001.rationale: It says people want to follow up and that single-turn question answering felt artificial.

r002.rationale: It says the model can ask for clarification instead of guessing, and users can clarify what they meant.

r003.rationale: It says the model already knew a great deal and browsing was mainly useful for recent events or specific facts, making it a distraction from the broader capability.

astra-6.text:
Well, WebGPT was already pretty close to an assistant. You asked it a question, it browsed the web, and it wrote an answer. But it was all one shot. If the answer wasn’t quite what you wanted, you couldn’t ask a follow-up or clarify your question. So making that conversational seemed like a natural extension.

And question answering is only one thing you might want from a language model. You might want help writing something, or working through a programming problem. A conversational interface gives you a pretty general way to do those things, because you can go back and forth and refine what you’re asking for.

r001.rationale: The response says WebGPT was one-shot and users could not ask follow-up questions, motivating a conversational interface.

r002.rationale: It says users could clarify their questions, but does not identify the model’s need to ask clarifying questions about ambiguity.

r003.rationale: The response gives no reason for deemphasizing browsing and does not mention the model’s internal knowledge.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, WebGPT was already pretty close to being an assistant. You’d ask it a question, and it would browse the web and write an answer. But it was a one-shot interaction. If it misunderstood what you wanted, or you wanted to dig into some part of the answer, you couldn’t just follow up naturally.

So conversation seemed like a pretty obvious extension. You want to be able to ask a question, see the response, and say, “Actually, I meant this,” or “Can you explain that part?” And the same basic approach—training on human demonstrations and then using human feedback—seemed like it ought to work for that more general setting.

r001.rationale: It says users wanted to “dig into” an answer and could not “follow up naturally,” then describes asking for an explanation.

r002.rationale: It points to cases where WebGPT misunderstood what the user wanted and gives “Actually, I meant this” as a natural clarification.

r003.rationale: The response gives no reason for deemphasizing browsing and says the assistant would browse the web; it does not mention strong internal knowledge.
